newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Two Russia hostages freed in Chechnya before talks.
newsitem.headline: Two Russia hostages freed in Chechnya before talks.

text.p: Two Russian journalists held hostage in Chechnya were freed on Sunday on the eve of tough talks in Moscow between President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov.

The kidnappers released their captives, who work for the private VID television channel, after Russian and Chechen security forces presented them with an ultimatum, Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov said.
"The criminals were made to understand that they would be destroyed if they did not comply with the ultimatum, so they released the journalists," he told Ekho Moskvy radio.
The journalists, seized in the breakaway region's capital Grozny on June 11, were expected to arrive in Moscow later on Sunday. Itar-Tass news agency said no ransom had been paid.
Their release came two days after security forces in Grozny rescued an ethnic Chechen hostage. A policeman was killed in that operation.
Yeltsin is expected to press Maskhadov during Monday's talks in the Kremlin to do more to help free the many Russian and foreign hostages seized in Chechnya by gunmen seeking ransoms.

Maskhadov, who has said hostage takers face the death penalty or tough prison sentences, convened a meeting of his security chiefs on Sunday to discuss the hostage issue, which has badly hampered his efforts to restore the rule of law.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those currently missing in Chechnya.

In Moscow Russian and Chechen negotiators continued to prepare the ground for Maskhadov's talks with Yeltsin but there was no sign that either side was prepared to modify its position over the key issue of Chechnya's political status.

Maskhadov made clear on Saturday he would not back off from his demand that Moscow recognise his tiny Caucasus region as a sovereign state. He said he wanted Russia and Chechnya to establish full-fledged diplomatic relations.

The Kremlin, whose troops were humiliated by Maskhadov's separatist guerrillas during a bloody 21-month conflict that ended last August, says Chechnya must stay within the Russian Federation, although with wide autonomy.
Ekho Moskvy radio on Sunday quoted an unnamed source in Russia's Security Council as saying Chechnya's demand for full-fledged diplomatic ties were unacceptable.
"Russia will do everything to prevent this from happening," he was quoted as saying.

Udugov told Ekho Moskvy that Yeltsin should take the initiative on Monday and recognise "the real situation" of Chechnya's independence. "Russia needs a reliable partner in the Caucasus, not a satellite," he said.
He also reiterated the Chechen demand that Moscow pay for the damage wreaked by its troops during the fighting.
"Russia is obliged by all moral norms to restore what it destroyed," he said. Chechnya puts the total cost of restoring its economy and infrastructure at a staggering $260 billion.
On Sunday Udugov and the Security Council's secretary, Ivan Rybkin, signed a protocol allowing family members of people missing in Chechnya to play a more active role in trying to locate them.
Rybkin has said the number of people still missing, including people taken captive during the war, totals 1,407.
